# Amazon RDS: questions

## Worked examples

<!-- quiz:start id=rds-q013 -->
### Question 1

A company runs an order service on a Single-AZ Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance. The company needs automatic failover that typically completes in under a minute if the primary fails. The company also wants the standby capacity to serve the dashboard read queries through a separate read-only endpoint, so that the dashboards stop loading the primary. Which deployment option will meet these requirements in the MOST operationally efficient way?

- Deploy a Multi-AZ DB cluster, send the writes to its writer endpoint, and send the dashboard queries to its reader endpoint.
- Deploy a Multi-AZ DB instance, and send the dashboard queries to the standby DB instance in the second Availability Zone.
- Keep the Single-AZ DB instance, add two read replicas for the dashboards, and run a script that promotes a replica on failure.
- Run PostgreSQL on three EC2 instances in three Availability Zones, with replication, failover and a read-only endpoint that the team manages.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Deploy a Multi-AZ DB cluster, send the writes to its writer endpoint, and send the dashboard queries to its reader endpoint.

**Deciding phrases.** "under a minute", "standby capacity to serve the dashboard read queries", "MOST operationally efficient"

**Think aloud.**

1. I read the last sentence first: it asks for the deployment option that is MOST operationally efficient.
2. I mark the constraints: RDS for PostgreSQL, automatic failover that typically finishes in under a minute, and standby capacity that serves the dashboard reads through a separate endpoint.
3. Before I look at the options, I predict a Multi-AZ DB cluster, because its two reader DB instances are automatic failover targets that also serve reads, and its failover typically takes under 35 seconds.
4. I remove the Multi-AZ DB instance, because its standby serves no reads and its failover typically takes 60 to 120 seconds. I remove the read replicas with a script, because a replica is promoted manually and promotion takes several minutes or longer.
5. Between the Multi-AZ DB cluster and PostgreSQL on EC2 the difference is who runs the replication and the failover; the stem says MOST operationally efficient, so the managed cluster wins over a design that the team builds and operates.
6. Check: the Multi-AZ DB cluster runs on PostgreSQL, fails over automatically in under a minute, serves the dashboards from its reader endpoint and needs no scripts. Time: 90 seconds.

**Why.** A Multi-AZ DB cluster runs a writer and [two reader DB instances](../facts/rds.md#rds-multi-az-cluster-three-azs-all-read) in [three separate Availability Zones](../facts/rds.md#rds-multi-az-cluster-three-azs-all-read), and [all three DB instances can serve read traffic](../facts/rds.md#rds-multi-az-cluster-three-azs-all-read). RDS runs the replication and the failover, so the cluster meets both needs as a managed option.

**Why not.**

- "Deploy a Multi-AZ DB instance, and send the ...": The standby [doesn't serve read traffic](../facts/rds.md#rds-multi-az-instance-standby-no-reads), and its failover typically takes [60–120 seconds](../facts/rds.md#rds-multi-az-instance-failover-time).
- "Keep the Single-AZ DB instance, add two read ...": A replica [can be manually promoted](../facts/rds.md#rds-compare-failover-vs-promote), and promotion takes [several minutes or longer](../facts/rds.md#rds-read-replica-promote-reboot-minutes), so the failover is slow.
- "Run PostgreSQL on three EC2 instances in three ...": It can work, but on EC2 the team owns the [upgrades, patches, backups, capacity planning](../facts/rds.md#rds-decision-guide-rehost-ec2-tasks) and the failover design.

**Twin.** If the stem said "failover within a few minutes, and the dashboards can stay on the primary" instead: a Multi-AZ DB instance, with failover in [60–120 seconds](../facts/rds.md#rds-multi-az-instance-failover-time).

**Takeaway.** Fast failover plus readable standbys on MySQL or PostgreSQL: a Multi-AZ DB cluster.

**Review.** [A Multi-AZ DB cluster has two readable standbys and fails over faster](2-deep.md#a-multi-az-db-cluster-has-two-readable-standbys-and-fails-over-faster-3-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 2

A company runs an encrypted Multi-AZ Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance in the us-east-1 Region. A customer managed AWS KMS key in us-east-1 encrypts the DB instance. A new contract requires cross-Region disaster recovery. If us-east-1 becomes unavailable, the company must run the database in us-west-2 from a copy with a recovery point of minutes, not hours. The copy must stay encrypted at rest. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)

- Rely on the Multi-AZ standby, because RDS fails over to the standby automatically if us-east-1 becomes unavailable.
- Create a cross-Region read replica of the DB instance in us-west-2, and promote the replica if us-east-1 becomes unavailable.
- Run MySQL on an Amazon EC2 instance in us-west-2, and manage binary log replication from the DB instance to it.
- Choose a KMS key in us-west-2 to encrypt the read replica when the company creates the replica in us-west-2.
- Use the ARN of the KMS key in us-east-1 for the read replica, so that both Regions use one key.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.**

- Create a cross-Region read replica of the DB instance in us-west-2, and promote the replica if us-east-1 becomes unavailable.
- Choose a KMS key in us-west-2 to encrypt the read replica when the company creates the replica in us-west-2.

**Deciding phrases.** "cross-Region disaster recovery", "a recovery point of minutes, not hours", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Think aloud.**

1. I read the last sentence first: it asks for two steps that together give recovery in another Region with the LEAST operational overhead.
2. I mark the constraints: an encrypted Multi-AZ DB instance in us-east-1, recovery in us-west-2 if us-east-1 becomes unavailable, a recovery point of minutes, and encryption at rest with a customer managed KMS key.
3. Before I look at the options, I predict that the Multi-AZ standby already covers this, because RDS fails over to the standby automatically.
4. I remove the MySQL database on an EC2 instance, because the team would run the database and the replication by hand. I remove the KMS key ARN from us-east-1, because KMS keys are specific to the Region where they are created.
5. Between the Multi-AZ standby and the cross-Region read replica the difference is the Region. My first idea breaks because the standby is in a different Availability Zone of the same Region, so the standby is lost together with us-east-1. The replica in us-west-2 replicates asynchronously, so its copy is minutes behind, and a replica can be promoted by hand. It needs a KMS key in us-west-2.
6. Check: the cross-Region read replica and the KMS key in us-west-2 meet every constraint, and nothing extra runs on EC2. Time: 90 seconds.

**Why.** Multi-AZ protects against [DB instance failure and Availability Zone disruption](../facts/rds.md#rds-multi-az-instance-protects-az-disruption), not against the loss of a Region. A cross-Region read replica is the managed copy in us-west-2. Because the source is encrypted, the company chooses a [KMS key in the destination AWS Region](../facts/rds.md#rds-cross-region-replica-encrypted-source-dest-key) for the replica.

- A DB instance that [replicates asynchronously to a standby DB instance](../facts/rds.md#rds-multi-region-async-replica-survives-region) in another Region keeps a copy there, and a replica [can be manually promoted](../facts/rds.md#rds-compare-failover-vs-promote).
- An encrypted replica in another Region needs a key there, so you [specify a KMS key in the destination Region](../facts/rds.md#rds-encryption-kms-regional-replica).

**Why not.**

- "Rely on the Multi-AZ standby, because RDS fails ...": RDS places the standby in [a different Availability Zone of the same Region](../facts/rds.md#rds-multi-az-standby-same-region), so the standby is lost together with us-east-1.
- "Run MySQL on an Amazon EC2 instance in ...": It can work, but the team then owns [upgrades, patches, backups, capacity planning](../facts/rds.md#rds-decision-guide-rehost-ec2-tasks) and the replication itself.
- "Use the ARN of the KMS key in ...": [KMS keys are specific to the AWS Region](../facts/rds.md#rds-encryption-kms-regional-replica) where they are created, so the us-east-1 key cannot encrypt the replica.

**Twin.** If the stem said "if one Availability Zone fails" instead: the existing Multi-AZ deployment is enough, because it gives [automatic failover to standby](../facts/rds.md#rds-compare-failover-vs-promote).

**Takeaway.** Region-level recovery needs a cross-Region read replica, encrypted with a KMS key in the destination Region.

**Review.** [A read replica in another Region can be promoted after a disaster](2-deep.md#a-read-replica-in-another-region-can-be-promoted-after-a-disaster-4-min)

</details>

### Question 3

A company runs a production application on Amazon EC2 instances across multiple Availability Zones. The application stores customer orders in one Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance, and analysts run long reporting queries against the same DB instance every month. The database must keep accepting writes, without losing committed data, if its Availability Zone fails. Which solution will meet this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Run PostgreSQL on two EC2 instances in two Availability Zones, with replication and failover that the team manages, and reports on the second instance.
- Modify the DB instance to a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment, and keep sending every query to the existing DB instance endpoint.
- Modify the DB instance to a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment, and send the reporting queries to the standby DB instance in the second Availability Zone.
- Create a read replica of the DB instance in a second Availability Zone, and send the reporting queries to the read replica endpoint.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Modify the DB instance to a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment, and keep sending every query to the existing DB instance endpoint.

**Deciding phrases.** "keep accepting writes, without losing committed data", "if its Availability Zone fails", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** In a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment, database writes are [concurrent on the primary and standby](../facts/rds.md#rds-faq-multiaz-replication-synchronous), so the standby holds every committed write. On a zone failure, RDS fails over and keeps the [name record for your DB instance](../facts/rds.md#rds-faq-multiaz-automatic-failover). The team turns it on [by modifying the DB instance](../facts/rds.md#rds-multi-az-convert-by-modifying) and runs no failover process.

**Why not.**

- "Run PostgreSQL on two EC2 instances in two ...": It can work, but on EC2 the team owns the [upgrades, patches, backups, capacity planning](../facts/rds.md#rds-decision-guide-rehost-ec2-tasks) and the failover itself.
- "Modify the DB instance to a Multi-AZ DB ...": The standby of a Multi-AZ DB instance [doesn't serve read traffic](../facts/rds.md#rds-multi-az-instance-standby-no-reads), so the reporting part of this design cannot work.
- "Create a read replica of the DB instance ...": A read replica [can be manually promoted](../facts/rds.md#rds-compare-failover-vs-promote), and for write availability AWS advises to [run your DB instance as a Multi-AZ deployment](../facts/rds.md#rds-faq-multi-az-for-write-availability).

**Twin.** If the stem said "The reporting queries must stop slowing down the order writes on the primary DB instance" instead: the read replica, because it serves [read-heavy database workloads](../facts/rds.md#rds-read-replica-definition).

**Takeaway.** Zone failure with no lost writes: Multi-AZ. Reports that slow the primary: a read replica.

**Review.** [A Multi-AZ DB instance copies every write to a standby synchronously](2-deep.md#a-multi-az-db-instance-copies-every-write-to-a-standby-synchronously-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 4

A company runs an order database on an Amazon RDS for MySQL Multi-AZ DB instance. Automated backups are turned on, with a backup retention period of 7 days. The company has no manual DB snapshots. Two hours ago, an engineer deleted a table by mistake. The company must recover the table as it was at a specific time, 5 minutes before the deletion. What should a solutions architect do to meet this requirement?

- Rely on the standby DB instance of the Multi-AZ deployment, which keeps a second copy of all of the data in another Availability Zone.
- Roll back the existing DB instance in place to an earlier point in time, so that the application can keep using the same endpoint.
- Restore the database to a point in time as a new DB instance, copy back the needed data, and delete the new instance.
- Take a manual DB snapshot of the DB instance now, and keep the snapshot until the company decides to delete it.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Restore the database to a point in time as a new DB instance, copy back the needed data, and delete the new instance.

**Deciding phrases.** "deleted a table by mistake", "5 minutes before the deletion", "backup retention period of 7 days"

**Why.** Automated backups enable [point-in-time recovery](../facts/rds.md#rds-faq-automated-backups-enable-pitr): RDS keeps a daily snapshot and the transaction logs. So RDS can recover [any point in time](../facts/rds.md#rds-automated-backup-pitr-in-retention) inside the 7-day retention period. The restore creates a new DB instance, and the team copies the table back from it.

**Why not.**

- "Rely on the standby DB instance of the ...": Writes are [concurrent on the primary and standby](../facts/rds.md#rds-faq-multiaz-replication-synchronous), so the standby lost the table at the same moment as the primary.
- "Roll back the existing DB instance in place ...": RDS restores by [creating a new DB instance](../facts/rds.md#rds-pitr-new-instance-within-retention), which is [created with a new endpoint](../facts/rds.md#rds-faq-restore-creates-new-instance); the existing DB instance stays as it is.
- "Take a manual DB snapshot of the DB ...": A snapshot taken now holds the database after the deletion, so the deleted table is missing from it.

**Twin.** If the stem said "retain a copy of the database as it is today for 7 years" instead: the manual snapshot, because manual snapshots are [kept until you explicitly delete them](../facts/rds.md#rds-faq-snapshots-user-initiated-kept-until-deleted).

**Takeaway.** Undo a recent mistake: a point-in-time restore to a new DB instance. Keep a copy for years: a manual snapshot.

**Review.** [Automated backups restore to any second inside the retention period](2-deep.md#automated-backups-restore-to-any-second-inside-the-retention-period-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 5

A web application on Amazon EC2 instances connects to an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL Multi-AZ DB instance. During a failover test, the application lost all its open database connections, and some clients kept using the old IP address of the database for several minutes. The company wants minimal downtime during future failovers, and it accepts only minimal code changes. Which solution will BEST meet these requirements?

- Make no change, because the DB instance endpoint name stays the same after a failover and the open connections move to the standby.
- Add connection retry logic to every application component, and lower the DNS cache time to live on every EC2 instance to a few seconds.
- Create an Amazon RDS Proxy for the DB instance, and change the database endpoint in the application configuration to the proxy endpoint.
- Create a read replica in a second Availability Zone, and send the application's writes to the read replica while a failover runs.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create an Amazon RDS Proxy for the DB instance, and change the database endpoint in the application configuration to the proxy endpoint.

**Deciding phrases.** "lost all its open database connections", "kept using the old IP address", "minimal code changes"

**Why.** RDS Proxy [bypasses Domain Name System (DNS) caches](../facts/rds-proxy.md#rds-proxy-faq-bypasses-dns-caches) and reduces failover times by [up to 66%](../facts/rds-proxy.md#rds-proxy-failover-66-percent) for Multi-AZ DB instances. Through the proxy, [most connections stay alive during failovers](../facts/rds-proxy.md#rds-proxy-failover-idle-connections-kept). The application changes one endpoint setting.

**Why not.**

- "Make no change, because the DB instance endpoint ...": At failover RDS [changes the Domain Name System (DNS) record](../facts/rds.md#rds-multi-az-failover-dns-change-reconnect), and the application must [re-establish any existing connections](../facts/rds.md#rds-multi-az-failover-dns-change-reconnect).
- "Add connection retry logic to every application component, ...": AWS advises to [implement database connection retry at the application layer](../facts/rds.md#rds-multi-az-cname-flip-retry), but this changes code in every component and still drops each open connection.
- "Create a read replica in a second Availability ...": Clients have [read-only access to the replica](../facts/rds.md#rds-read-replica-async-read-only), and RDS does not allow a PostgreSQL read replica [to be made writable](../facts/rds.md#rds-replica-postgresql-not-writable).

**Twin.** If the stem said "the application must keep connecting directly to the database" instead: retry logic and a DNS cache time to live of [less than 30 seconds](../facts/rds.md#rds-bp-dns-ttl-under-30-seconds).

**Takeaway.** Failover drops connections and DNS caches lag: put RDS Proxy in front of the DB instance.

**Review.** [RDS Proxy keeps client connections open while the database fails over](2-deep.md#rds-proxy-keeps-client-connections-open-while-the-database-fails-over-3-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 6

A company runs a production application on Amazon EC2 instances across multiple Availability Zones. The application stores customer orders in one Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance, and analysts run long reporting queries against the same DB instance every month. The reporting queries must stop slowing down the order writes on the primary DB instance. Which solution will meet this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Run PostgreSQL on two EC2 instances in two Availability Zones, with replication and failover that the team manages, and reports on the second instance.
- Modify the DB instance to a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment, and keep sending every query to the existing DB instance endpoint.
- Modify the DB instance to a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment, and send the reporting queries to the standby DB instance in the second Availability Zone.
- Create a read replica of the DB instance in a second Availability Zone, and send the reporting queries to the read replica endpoint.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create a read replica of the DB instance in a second Availability Zone, and send the reporting queries to the read replica endpoint.

**Deciding phrases.** "reporting queries must stop slowing down the order writes", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** A read replica is a [read-only copy of a DB instance](../facts/rds.md#rds-read-replica-definition). RDS takes the updates of the primary and [copies them asynchronously to the read replica](../facts/rds.md#rds-read-replica-async-read-only). The reporting queries move to the replica endpoint, and the primary keeps its capacity for the order writes. RDS creates and maintains the replica, so the team runs no replication software.

**Why not.**

- "Run PostgreSQL on two EC2 instances in two ...": It can work, but on EC2 the team owns the [upgrades, patches, backups, capacity planning](../facts/rds.md#rds-decision-guide-rehost-ec2-tasks) and the replication itself.
- "Modify the DB instance to a Multi-AZ DB ...": A Multi-AZ DB instance [isn't a scaling solution for read-only scenarios](../facts/rds.md#rds-multi-az-instance-not-read-scaling), so the reports still run on the primary.
- "Modify the DB instance to a Multi-AZ DB ...": The standby of a Multi-AZ DB instance [doesn't serve read traffic](../facts/rds.md#rds-multi-az-instance-standby-no-reads), so the reports cannot move to it.

**Twin.** If the stem said "The database must keep accepting writes, without losing committed data, if its Availability Zone fails" instead: Multi-AZ, which protects against [DB instance failure and Availability Zone disruption](../facts/rds.md#rds-multi-az-instance-protects-az-disruption).

**Takeaway.** Reports that slow the primary: a read replica. A Multi-AZ DB instance standby serves no reads.

**Review.** [A read replica receives changes later and serves only reads](2-deep.md#a-read-replica-receives-changes-later-and-serves-only-reads-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 7

A company runs a web application on three Amazon EC2 instances in one Availability Zone. The application stores its data in a Single-AZ Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance in the same Availability Zone. The company must make the application highly available, so that it keeps working if one Availability Zone fails. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)

- Launch three more EC2 instances in the same Availability Zone, and put an Application Load Balancer in front of all six instances.
- Create an Auto Scaling group that launches the instances across two Availability Zones behind an Application Load Balancer.
- Create a read replica of the DB instance in the same Availability Zone, and point the application to the replica if the primary fails.
- Install MySQL on an EC2 instance in a second Availability Zone, and run replication and failover scripts that the team maintains.
- Modify the DB instance to a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment, so that RDS keeps a synchronous standby in a second Availability Zone.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.**

- Create an Auto Scaling group that launches the instances across two Availability Zones behind an Application Load Balancer.
- Modify the DB instance to a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment, so that RDS keeps a synchronous standby in a second Availability Zone.

**Deciding phrases.** "highly available", "if one Availability Zone fails", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** Both tiers sit in the zone that can fail, so both need a second zone. EC2 Auto Scaling [maintains balance across all of the Availability Zones](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-desired-spread-across-azs) of the group. A Multi-AZ DB instance protects against [DB instance failure and Availability Zone disruption](../facts/rds.md#rds-multi-az-instance-protects-az-disruption), and RDS runs the failover.

- With two zones, the [desired capacity is distributed across these Availability Zones](../facts/ec2-auto-scaling.md#ec2-auto-scaling-desired-spread-across-azs), so instances keep running when one zone fails.
- RDS keeps a [synchronous standby replica in a different Availability Zone](../facts/rds.md#rds-multi-az-instance-standby-no-reads) and has [automatic failover to standby](../facts/rds.md#rds-compare-failover-vs-promote).

**Why not.**

- "Launch three more EC2 instances in the same ...": Every instance stays in the zone that can fail, and an Application Load Balancer needs [at least two Availability Zone subnets](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-subnets-two-azs-different).
- "Create a read replica of the DB instance ...": The replica sits in the same zone, and a replica [can be manually promoted](../facts/rds.md#rds-compare-failover-vs-promote) instead of failing over by itself.
- "Install MySQL on an EC2 instance in a ...": It can work, but the team then owns the [upgrades, patches, backups, capacity planning](../facts/rds.md#rds-decision-guide-rehost-ec2-tasks) and the failover scripts.

**Twin.** If the stem said "if the whole AWS Region fails" instead: a copy in a second Region, such as a cross-Region read replica, which stays available [if one Region becomes unavailable](../facts/rds.md#rds-multi-region-async-replica-survives-region).

**Takeaway.** High availability puts every tier in two zones: an Auto Scaling group behind a load balancer, and Multi-AZ RDS.

**Review.** [A Multi-AZ DB instance copies every write to a standby synchronously](2-deep.md#a-multi-az-db-instance-copies-every-write-to-a-standby-synchronously-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 8

A company runs an order database on an Amazon RDS for MySQL Multi-AZ DB instance. Automated backups are turned on, with a backup retention period of 7 days. The company has no manual DB snapshots. A new regulation mandates that the company retain a copy of the database as it is today for 7 years. What should a solutions architect do to meet this requirement?

- Rely on the standby DB instance of the Multi-AZ deployment, which keeps a second copy of all of the data in another Availability Zone.
- Roll back the existing DB instance in place to an earlier point in time, so that the application can keep using the same endpoint.
- Restore the database to a point in time as a new DB instance, copy back the needed data, and delete the new instance.
- Take a manual DB snapshot of the DB instance now, and keep the snapshot until the company decides to delete it.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Take a manual DB snapshot of the DB instance now, and keep the snapshot until the company decides to delete it.

**Deciding phrases.** "retain a copy of the database as it is today", "for 7 years"

**Why.** Manual DB snapshots are [kept until you explicitly delete them](../facts/rds.md#rds-faq-snapshots-user-initiated-kept-until-deleted), while automated backups last [between 0 and 35 days](../facts/rds.md#rds-backup-retention-range). A snapshot taken now holds the database as it is today, and it outlives the 7-day automated backups, so it meets the regulation.

**Why not.**

- "Rely on the standby DB instance of the ...": The standby changes with every write, because writes are [concurrent on the primary and standby](../facts/rds.md#rds-faq-multiaz-replication-synchronous), so it keeps no copy of the database as it is today.
- "Roll back the existing DB instance in place ...": RDS restores by [creating a new DB instance](../facts/rds.md#rds-pitr-new-instance-within-retention), not by a rollback in place, and a rollback would keep no copy for 7 years.
- "Restore the database to a point in time ...": The new DB instance is deleted at the end, so nothing is kept, and automated backups are kept for [between 0 and 35 days](../facts/rds.md#rds-backup-retention-range).

**Twin.** If the stem said "Two hours ago, an engineer deleted a table by mistake" instead: the point-in-time restore to a new DB instance, which reaches [any second during your retention period](../facts/rds.md#rds-faq-pitr-any-second-latest-restorable).

**Takeaway.** Keep a copy for years: a manual snapshot. Automated backups expire with their retention period.

**Review.** [Manual snapshots stay until you delete them and can leave the Region](2-deep.md#manual-snapshots-stay-until-you-delete-them-and-can-leave-the-region-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 9

An audit finds that a company's Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance was created without encryption. The company must encrypt the data at rest with an AWS KMS key, and the encryption must also cover the automated backups and any future read replicas. A short maintenance window for the cutover is acceptable. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Modify the DB instance to turn on encryption with the KMS key, and apply the change during the next maintenance window.
- Create a read replica of the DB instance that is encrypted with the KMS key, and promote the replica to a standalone DB instance.
- Take a snapshot, copy the snapshot with encryption under the KMS key, and restore a new DB instance from the encrypted copy.
- Create a new encrypted DB instance with the KMS key, and move the data with a dump and restore that the team scripts and runs.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Take a snapshot, copy the snapshot with encryption under the KMS key, and restore a new DB instance from the encrypted copy.

**Deciding phrases.** "was created without encryption", "encrypt the data at rest with an AWS KMS key", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** RDS encrypts a DB instance at creation, [not after the DB instance is created](../facts/rds.md#rds-encryption-only-at-create), so the fix is a new, encrypted DB instance. An encrypted snapshot copy creates it without scripts. After the restore, encryption covers the [logs, automated backups, read replicas, and snapshots](../facts/rds.md#rds-encryption-at-rest-scope). The application moves to the new endpoint in the maintenance window.

**Why not.**

- "Modify the DB instance to turn on encryption ...": You can [only encrypt an Amazon RDS DB instance](../facts/rds.md#rds-encryption-only-at-create) when you create it, so a modification cannot turn encryption on.
- "Create a read replica of the DB instance ...": For an encrypted read replica, [the source DB instance must be encrypted](../facts/rds.md#rds-read-replica-encrypted-needs-encrypted-source), and this source is not encrypted.
- "Create a new encrypted DB instance with the ...": It works, but the team writes, tests and runs the dump and the restore, which a snapshot copy does without scripts.

**Twin.** If the stem said "a DB instance that the company will create next month" instead: turn on encryption at creation, because RDS encrypts a DB instance then and [not after the DB instance is created](../facts/rds.md#rds-encryption-only-at-create).

**Takeaway.** To encrypt an existing DB instance, copy a snapshot with encryption and restore a new DB instance.

**Review.** [Encryption at rest is chosen at creation and covers every copy](2-deep.md#encryption-at-rest-is-chosen-at-creation-and-covers-every-copy-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=rds-q006 -->
### Question 10

A company is moving a legacy packaged application from its data center to AWS. The application uses a Microsoft SQL Server database. The software vendor supports the application only when the vendor's monitoring agent runs on the operating system of the database host. The company wants AWS to automate as much database administration as possible, such as backups and patching. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Run the database on Amazon RDS for SQL Server, and install the vendor's agent on the host of the DB instance.
- Run SQL Server on Amazon EC2 instances that the team manages, and install the vendor's agent on each instance.
- Move the database to Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL, and run the vendor's agent on an EC2 instance next to the cluster.
- Run the database on Amazon RDS Custom for SQL Server, and install the vendor's agent on the DB instance host.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Run the database on Amazon RDS Custom for SQL Server, and install the vendor's agent on the DB instance host.

**Deciding phrases.** "agent runs on the operating system of the database host", "automate as much database administration as possible", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** The vendor needs access to the operating system, and the company wants managed administration. RDS Custom automates database administration and lets you [customize your database environment and operating system](../facts/rds.md#rds-custom-os-access). AWS says that [Amazon RDS Custom is the better choice](../facts/rds.md#rds-custom-vs-rds-vs-ec2) when you need administrative rights to the database and the underlying operating system.

**Why not.**

- "Run the database on Amazon RDS for SQL ...": Standard Amazon RDS [doesn't let you access the underlying host](../facts/rds.md#rds-custom-os-access), so the vendor's agent has no place to run.
- "Run SQL Server on Amazon EC2 instances that ...": It works, but with SQL Server on EC2 the team owns [upgrades, patches, backups, capacity planning](../facts/rds.md#rds-decision-guide-rehost-ec2-tasks).
- "Move the database to Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL, and ...": The packaged application is built for SQL Server, and an agent on a separate EC2 instance is not on the database host.

**Twin.** If the stem said "The vendor supports the application on any managed SQL Server database" instead: Amazon RDS for SQL Server, because the agent is not needed and standard RDS leaves less administration to the team.

**Takeaway.** Host access plus managed administration points to RDS Custom; full control points to EC2.

**Review.** [Amazon RDS runs the database engine while you keep the queries](2-deep.md#amazon-rds-runs-the-database-engine-while-you-keep-the-queries-3-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=rds-q002 -->
### Question 11

A company runs an order database on an Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance with General Purpose SSD storage. Twice last quarter, the allocated storage filled up, and the application could not write new orders until an engineer added storage. The data grows at an unpredictable rate. The company does not want to pay in advance for a large amount of storage that it does not use. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm on free storage space that invokes an AWS Lambda function to increase the allocated storage.
- Allocate twice the current storage now, and reduce the allocated storage again after the company deletes old orders each year.
- Change the storage type to Provisioned IOPS SSD, so that busy write periods no longer fill the allocated storage.
- Turn on storage autoscaling for the DB instance, and set a maximum storage threshold that fits the company's budget.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Turn on storage autoscaling for the DB instance, and set a maximum storage threshold that fits the company's budget.

**Deciding phrases.** "the allocated storage filled up", "grows at an unpredictable rate", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** Storage autoscaling is the RDS feature for this case, and AWS points to it [if your workload is unpredictable](../facts/rds.md#rds-storage-autoscaling-unpredictable). Turning it on [doesn't cause any downtime](../facts/rds.md#rds-storage-autoscaling-no-downtime). Storage grows in steps as the data grows, so the company does not pay for a large reserve in advance, and the team does not watch the free space.

**Why not.**

- "Create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm on free storage ...": It works, but the team builds and maintains the alarm and the function, which storage autoscaling does without any code.
- "Allocate twice the current storage now, and reduce ...": Allocated storage cannot shrink, because [you can't deallocate space](../facts/rds.md#rds-storage-increase-min-10-percent), so the extra storage stays and the company pays for it.
- "Change the storage type to Provisioned IOPS SSD, ...": Provisioned IOPS gives [low I/O latency and consistent I/O throughput](../facts/rds.md#rds-storage-piops-for-production), not more space, so the storage still fills.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the database needs faster, more consistent storage, not more space" instead: Provisioned IOPS storage, because it gives [low I/O latency and consistent I/O throughput](../facts/rds.md#rds-storage-piops-for-production).

**Takeaway.** Storage that fills at an unpredictable rate points to storage autoscaling with a maximum threshold.

**Review.** [Storage autoscaling grows storage before it fills but never shrinks it](2-deep.md#storage-autoscaling-grows-storage-before-it-fills-but-never-shrinks-it-3-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 12

A company runs a mission-critical transactional (OLTP) database on Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL. The DB instance uses a general-purpose instance class and General Purpose SSD (gp3) storage. At peak, the workload performs many small random writes, and commit times vary with the storage response time. The company needs consistent, low storage latency for this workload. Which storage configuration will provide the LOWEST latency for the database storage?

- Keep General Purpose SSD (gp3) storage, and turn on storage autoscaling so that RDS adds storage before each peak.
- Move the storage to a larger General Purpose SSD (gp2) volume, so that the baseline IOPS grow with the volume size.
- Move the storage to Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2 Block Express), and provision the IOPS rate that the peak workload needs.
- Change the DB instance to a memory-optimized instance class, and keep the General Purpose SSD (gp3) storage as it is.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Move the storage to Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2 Block Express), and provision the IOPS rate that the peak workload needs.

**Deciding phrases.** "consistent, low storage latency", "many small random writes", "LOWEST latency"

**Why.** Provisioned IOPS storage is built for [low I/O latency and consistent I/O throughput](../facts/rds.md#rds-storage-piops-for-production). Each commit waits for the storage, so the storage type sets the commit time. More memory or more capacity leaves the gp3 latency class as it is.

**Why not.**

- "Keep General Purpose SSD (gp3) storage, and turn ...": When free space runs low, [it automatically scales up your storage](../facts/rds.md#rds-storage-autoscaling-unpredictable), but gp3 latency stays [single-digit millisecond, provided consistently 99% of the time](../facts/rds.md#rds-storage-latency-by-type).
- "Move the storage to a larger General Purpose ...": The gp2 baseline grows at [3 IOPS for each GiB](../facts/rds.md#rds-storage-gp2-baseline-per-gib), but its latency stays [single-digit millisecond, provided consistently 99% of the time](../facts/rds.md#rds-storage-latency-by-type).
- "Change the DB instance to a memory-optimized instance ...": More memory helps reads when the working set [resides almost completely in memory](../facts/rds.md#rds-bp-working-set-in-memory), but each commit still waits for the gp3 storage.

**Twin.** If the stem said "a development database with moderate I/O and a small budget" instead: General Purpose SSD (gp3), which is [best suited for development and testing environments](../facts/rds.md#rds-storage-gp-for-dev-test).

**Takeaway.** Consistent sub-millisecond storage latency for OLTP: Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2 Block Express).

**Review.** [The instance class sets compute and the storage type sets IOPS](2-deep.md#the-instance-class-sets-compute-and-the-storage-type-sets-iops-3-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=rds-q019 -->
### Question 13

A company runs a production database on an Amazon RDS for MySQL Multi-AZ DB instance. The company must upgrade the database to a new major engine version. Before the switch, the team wants to test the new version on a copy of the database that stays in sync with production. The switch must cause minimal downtime. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Upgrade the engine version in place, because the Multi-AZ deployment upgrades the standby first and then fails over to it.
- Take a DB snapshot, restore it to a new DB instance, upgrade the new DB instance, and move the application to it.
- Use AWS Database Migration Service to replicate the data to a new DB instance on the new version, test it, and then cut over.
- Create an Amazon RDS Blue/Green Deployment, upgrade the green environment to the new version, test it, and then switch over.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create an Amazon RDS Blue/Green Deployment, upgrade the green environment to the new version, test it, and then switch over.

**Deciding phrases.** "stays in sync with production", "minimal downtime", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** An engine upgrade needs downtime, [even for Multi-AZ instances](../facts/rds.md#rds-faq-upgrade-downtime-even-multiaz), and AWS advises to minimize it by [using a blue/green deployment](../facts/rds.md#rds-engine-upgrade-downtime-blue-green). The switch has [short, predictable downtime](../facts/rds.md#rds-faq-blue-green-use-cases), and RDS keeps the green copy in sync, so the team runs no replication of its own.

**Why not.**

- "Upgrade the engine version in place, because the ...": An engine upgrade [modifies both primary and secondary DB instances](../facts/rds.md#rds-multi-az-engine-upgrade-both-down), and it [causes downtime until the upgrade is complete](../facts/rds.md#rds-multi-az-engine-upgrade-both-down).
- "Take a DB snapshot, restore it to a ...": A copy made by [restoring from the DB snapshot](../facts/rds.md#rds-faq-test-upgrade-on-restored-copy) is good for a test, but it receives no production writes after the snapshot.
- "Use AWS Database Migration Service to replicate the ...": It can work, but the team builds, runs and cuts over the replication itself, which a blue/green deployment does for the team.

**Twin.** If the stem said "a minor engine version, and a short outage in the maintenance window is acceptable" instead: an in-place upgrade with [Auto Minor Version Upgrade](../facts/rds.md#rds-faq-auto-minor-version-upgrade).

**Takeaway.** Major upgrade, tested on a synced copy, short switch: an RDS Blue/Green Deployment.

**Review.** [A Multi-AZ DB instance copies every write to a standby synchronously](2-deep.md#a-multi-az-db-instance-copies-every-write-to-a-standby-synchronously-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=rds-q017 -->
### Question 14

A development team uses an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance for testing from 08:00 to 18:00 on weekdays. The schedule is predictable, and nobody uses the DB instance at night or on weekends. The data in the database must stay between working days, and the team wants no manual steps each day. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?

- Stop the DB instance every Friday evening and start it every Monday morning, and keep it running on weekday nights.
- Use an automated schedule that stops the DB instance every evening and starts it again every working morning.
- Buy a three-year Reserved DB instance for the instance class, and keep the DB instance running all day, every day.
- Delete the DB instance every evening without a final snapshot, and restore it every morning from its automated backups.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Use an automated schedule that stops the DB instance every evening and starts it again every working morning.

**Deciding phrases.** "nobody uses the DB instance at night or on weekends", "The data in the database must stay", "MOST cost-effective way"

**Why.** The DB instance is idle every night and every weekend. RDS bills a stopped DB instance for storage [but not for DB instance hours](../facts/rds.md#rds-faq-billing-stopped-instance), so a daily stop and start removes the instance cost of every idle period. A schedule does this with no manual steps, and the data stays in the stopped DB instance.

**Why not.**

- "Stop the DB instance every Friday evening and ...": It removes the weekend hours. A stopped DB instance is billed for storage [but not for DB instance hours](../facts/rds.md#rds-faq-billing-stopped-instance), and this design still pays for every weekday night.
- "Buy a three-year Reserved DB instance for the ...": A reservation is a [one or three year term](../facts/rds.md#rds-faq-ri-terms-one-or-three-year) commitment that pays for every hour, but this DB instance is idle most hours of each week.
- "Delete the DB instance every evening without a ...": Without a final snapshot, [all automated backups are deleted](../facts/rds.md#rds-delete-instance-automated-backups-deleted) with the DB instance, so nothing is left to restore in the morning.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the database serves production traffic all day, every day" instead: a Reserved DB instance, a [one or three year term](../facts/rds.md#rds-faq-ri-terms-one-or-three-year) commitment for steady use.

**Takeaway.** Idle every night and weekend on a known schedule: stop and start the DB instance automatically.

**Review.** [The instance class sets compute and the storage type sets IOPS](2-deep.md#the-instance-class-sets-compute-and-the-storage-type-sets-iops-3-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=rds-q012 -->
### Question 15

A company's web application stores its data in a Single-AZ Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance. The company wants to fix a performance problem without any change to the application's SQL queries. During spiky traffic, thousands of short-lived AWS Lambda invocations open connections, and the database returns too many connections errors at low CPU use. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Put Amazon RDS Proxy in front of the DB instance, and change the application's connection settings to use the proxy endpoint.
- Create a read replica of the DB instance, and change the application's connection settings to send its read-only queries to the replica.
- Move the database to PostgreSQL on Amazon EC2 instances, and run a connection pooler and streaming read replicas that the team manages.
- Modify the DB instance to a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment, so that the standby instance also serves part of the query load.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Put Amazon RDS Proxy in front of the DB instance, and change the application's connection settings to use the proxy endpoint.

**Deciding phrases.** "thousands of short-lived AWS Lambda invocations open connections", "too many connections errors at low CPU use", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** The errors come from the number of connections, not from CPU. Lambda functions benefit from the [connection pooling offered by RDS Proxy](../facts/rds-proxy.md#rds-proxy-lambda-connection-pooling). With multiplexing, the proxy [keeps a smaller number of connections open](../facts/rds-proxy.md#rds-proxy-multiplexing-fewer-db-connections) to the DB instance, so the connection errors become less likely without a larger instance.

**Why not.**

- "Create a read replica of the DB instance, ...": A replica takes reads, but each Lambda environment still opens its own connection, and high concurrency can [exhaust database connection limits](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-vpc-db-connections-rds-proxy) again.
- "Move the database to PostgreSQL on Amazon EC2 ...": A self-managed pooler works, but on EC2 the team owns [upgrades, patches, backups, capacity planning](../facts/rds.md#rds-decision-guide-rehost-ec2-tasks) of the database.
- "Modify the DB instance to a Multi-AZ DB ...": The standby [doesn't serve read traffic](../facts/rds.md#rds-multi-az-instance-standby-no-reads), and a Multi-AZ deployment does not pool the connections of the functions.

**Twin.** If the stem said "Dashboard read queries keep the CPU use near 90 percent at peak, but the number of database connections stays low" instead: a read replica, because it serves [read-heavy database workloads](../facts/rds.md#rds-read-replica-definition).

**Takeaway.** Connection errors at low CPU point to RDS Proxy; heavy reads point to a read replica.

**Review.** [RDS Proxy shares a small pool of connections among many clients](2-deep.md#rds-proxy-shares-a-small-pool-of-connections-among-many-clients-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=rds-q022 -->
### Question 16

A company runs an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance on a general-purpose instance class. Every afternoon, queries slow down. Amazon CloudWatch shows moderate CPU use, low freeable memory, and read IOPS that are high and keep rising under load. The number of connections is steady and far below the limit. A short outage in the next maintenance window is acceptable. Which change is the MOST operationally efficient way to solve the problem?

- Put Amazon RDS Proxy in front of the DB instance, so that the queries use pooled connections and need less memory.
- Modify the DB instance to a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment, so that the standby takes part of the read load.
- Modify the DB instance to a memory-optimized instance class of a similar size during the next maintenance window.
- Add an Amazon ElastiCache cluster, and change the application code to cache the results of the most frequent queries.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Modify the DB instance to a memory-optimized instance class of a similar size during the next maintenance window.

**Deciding phrases.** "low freeable memory", "read IOPS that are high and keep rising under load", "MOST operationally efficient"

**Why.** Low freeable memory and rising read IOPS mean that the working set no longer fits in memory. AWS advises enough RAM so that the working set [resides almost completely in memory](../facts/rds.md#rds-bp-working-set-in-memory). Memory-optimized classes such as db.z1d are [optimized for memory-intensive applications](../facts/rds.md#rds-class-memory-optimized-memory-intensive). The class change makes the database [temporarily unavailable](../facts/rds.md#rds-faq-compute-scale-brief-outage) for a short time, which the stem accepts.

**Why not.**

- "Put Amazon RDS Proxy in front of the ...": The proxy can [pool and share database connections](../facts/rds-proxy.md#rds-proxy-definition-pool-share), but connections are steady here, and the queries still read the same data from storage.
- "Modify the DB instance to a Multi-AZ DB ...": The standby of a Multi-AZ DB instance [doesn't serve read traffic](../facts/rds.md#rds-multi-az-instance-standby-no-reads), so the reads stay on the primary.
- "Add an Amazon ElastiCache cluster, and change the ...": A cache can lower the reads, but developers change the code and the team runs a cache cluster, which a class change avoids.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the database returns too many connections errors at low CPU use" instead: RDS Proxy, because it keeps a [smaller number of long-lived connections](../facts/rds-proxy.md#rds-proxy-candidate-too-many-connections).

**Takeaway.** Low freeable memory with rising read IOPS points to a memory-optimized instance class.

**Review.** [The instance class sets compute and the storage type sets IOPS](2-deep.md#the-instance-class-sets-compute-and-the-storage-type-sets-iops-3-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=rds-q016 -->
### Question 17

A company's web application stores its data in a Single-AZ Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance. The company wants to fix a performance problem without any change to the application's SQL queries. Dashboard read queries keep the CPU use near 90 percent at peak, but the number of database connections stays low. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Put Amazon RDS Proxy in front of the DB instance, and change the application's connection settings to use the proxy endpoint.
- Create a read replica of the DB instance, and change the application's connection settings to send its read-only queries to the replica.
- Move the database to PostgreSQL on Amazon EC2 instances, and run a connection pooler and streaming read replicas that the team manages.
- Modify the DB instance to a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment, so that the standby instance also serves part of the query load.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create a read replica of the DB instance, and change the application's connection settings to send its read-only queries to the replica.

**Deciding phrases.** "Dashboard read queries keep the CPU use near 90 percent", "the number of database connections stays low", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** The load comes from read queries, and the connections are few. A read replica is a [read-only copy of a DB instance](../facts/rds.md#rds-read-replica-definition), made for [read-heavy database workloads](../facts/rds.md#rds-read-replica-definition). The dashboards send their queries to the replica endpoint, and the primary keeps its CPU for the rest of the application.

**Why not.**

- "Put Amazon RDS Proxy in front of the ...": The proxy can [pool and share database connections](../facts/rds-proxy.md#rds-proxy-definition-pool-share), but connections are not the problem here, and each read query still runs on the DB instance.
- "Move the database to PostgreSQL on Amazon EC2 ...": Self-managed replicas can take the reads, but on EC2 the team owns [upgrades, patches, backups, capacity planning](../facts/rds.md#rds-decision-guide-rehost-ec2-tasks) of the database.
- "Modify the DB instance to a Multi-AZ DB ...": The standby of a Multi-AZ DB instance [doesn't serve read traffic](../facts/rds.md#rds-multi-az-instance-standby-no-reads), so the CPU load on the primary stays the same.

**Twin.** If the stem said "During spiky traffic, thousands of short-lived AWS Lambda invocations open connections, and the database returns too many connections errors at low CPU use" instead: RDS Proxy, because it pools [frequent short database connections](../facts/rds-proxy.md#rds-proxy-lambda-connection-pooling).

**Takeaway.** High read CPU with few connections points to a read replica, not to RDS Proxy or Multi-AZ.

**Review.** [A read replica receives changes later and serves only reads](2-deep.md#a-read-replica-receives-changes-later-and-serves-only-reads-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=rds-q018 -->
### Question 18

A company is choosing a database engine for a new application on Amazon RDS. The company's reporting team needs a read replica of the production database. On the replica, the team must create its own indexes and summary tables with DDL statements, and the replica must keep receiving all changes from the source DB instance. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST development effort?

- Use Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL, create a read replica, and make the replica writable for the reporting team's DDL statements.
- Use a Multi-AZ DB cluster of Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL, and run the DDL statements through the reader endpoint of the cluster.
- Use Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL, and build a job that copies every change from the DB instance into a separate reporting DB instance.
- Use Amazon RDS for MySQL, create a read replica, and set the read_only parameter of the replica to 0.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Use Amazon RDS for MySQL, create a read replica, and set the read_only parameter of the replica to 0.

**Deciding phrases.** "create its own indexes and summary tables with DDL statements", "keep receiving all changes from the source DB instance", "LEAST development effort"

**Why.** The deciding need is DDL on a replica that keeps replicating. RDS for MariaDB and MySQL replicas use logical replication, and you can enable a MySQL [read replica to be writable](../facts/rds.md#rds-replica-mysql-logical-writable). After this parameter change on the replica, the team adds its indexes and tables there, and changes from the source keep arriving.

**Why not.**

- "Use Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL, create a read ...": AWS does not allow an RDS for PostgreSQL read replica [to be made writable](../facts/rds.md#rds-replica-postgresql-not-writable), so the DDL statements fail.
- "Use a Multi-AZ DB cluster of Amazon RDS ...": The reader instances behind the reader endpoint [support only read operations](../facts/rds.md#rds-multi-az-cluster-writer-reader-endpoints), so DDL statements there fail.
- "Use Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL, and build a ...": A custom copy job works, but developers write, test and run the job, which a writable MySQL replica makes unnecessary.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the team runs only SELECT queries on the replica" instead: either engine fits, because every read replica gives [read-only access to the replica](../facts/rds.md#rds-read-replica-async-read-only).

**Takeaway.** DDL on a replica that keeps replicating points to RDS for MySQL or MariaDB, not to RDS for PostgreSQL.

**Review.** [A read replica receives changes later and serves only reads](2-deep.md#a-read-replica-receives-changes-later-and-serves-only-reads-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->
